sentence.en: The country's army consists of soldiers and officers.

en hættetrøje.explanation: "En hættetrøje" means "a hoodie". It is built from "en hætte" (a hood) and "en trøje" (a sweater). The part "trøje" also names a team shirt, such as "en fodboldtrøje" (a soccer jersey).

sentence.da: Det er koldt, og jeg tager min **hættetrøje** på.
sentence.en: It is cold, and I am putting on my hoodie.

en hæveautomat.explanation: "En hæveautomat" means "an ATM". It is built from "at hæve" (to withdraw) and "en automat" (a machine). To say you need cash, use "at hæve penge" (to withdraw money): "Jeg skal hæve penge" (I need to withdraw money).

sentence.da: Jeg henter penge i en **hæveautomat**.
sentence.en: I get money from an ATM.

en højde.explanation: "En højde" means "a height". To ask someone how tall they are, say: "Hvad er din højde?" (What is your height?)

sentence.da: Bjerget har en **højde** på tusind meter.
sentence.en: The mountain has a height of a thousand meters.

en højhed.explanation: "En højhed" means "a highness". It is a formal title for members of a royal family, used in "Hendes Kongelige Højhed" (Her Royal Highness) and "Hans Kongelige Højhed" (His Royal Highness). The ending "hed" turns an adjective into a noun, as in "en frihed" (a freedom).

sentence.da: Ordet **højhed** bruges som titel for medlemmer af kongehuset.
sentence.en: The word highness is used as a title for members of the royal family.

en højskole.explanation: "En højskole" means "a folk high school". It is a Danish school where people live together and take courses, with no exams. Do not mix it up with "et universitet" (a university): "Hun læser på universitetet" (She studies at the university).

related.en: a primary and lower secondary school

sentence.da: Hun bor på en **højskole** og synger i kor hver dag.
sentence.en: She lives at a folk high school and sings in a choir every day.

en højtid.explanation: "En højtid" means "a holiday (religious or major)". The big ones in Denmark are "jul" (Christmas), "påske" (Easter) and "pinse" (Whitsun).

sentence.da: Jul er den **højtid**, hvor familien samles.
sentence.en: Christmas is the holiday when the family gathers.

en højttaler.explanation: "En højttaler" means "a speaker". Do not mix it up with "en taler" (a person who gives a speech): "Taleren var god" (The speaker was good).

sentence.da: Musikken kommer fra min nye **højttaler**.
sentence.en: The music comes from my new speaker.

en høne.explanation: "En høne" means "a hen". To talk about chickens as a group, use "høns": "Vi har høns i haven" (We have chickens in the garden).

sentence.da: En **høne** bor i hønsehuset sammen med hanen.
sentence.en: A hen lives in the chicken coop with the rooster.

en hønsegård.explanation: "En hønsegård" means "a chicken yard". It is built from "høns" (chickens) and "en gård" (a yard). The word "gård" also means "a farm": "Vi bor på en gård" (We live on a farm).

sentence.da: Hønsene løber rundt i vores store **hønsegård**.
sentence.en: The chickens run around in our big chicken yard.

en høring.explanation: "En høring" means "a hearing". It comes from the verb "at høre" (to hear). A very common phrase is "at sende i høring" (to send out for comment): "Loven er sendt i høring" (The law has been sent out for comment).

sentence.da: Kommunen holder en **høring**, før den bygger den nye vej.
sentence.en: The municipality holds a hearing before it builds the new road.

en høst.explanation: "En høst" means "a harvest". It is the noun for the verb "at høste" (to harvest). To say farmers gather the crop, use the verb: "Bønderne høster kornet" (The farmers harvest the grain).

sentence.da: Bønderne er glade, når årets **høst** er stor og god.
sentence.en: The farmers are happy when this year's harvest is big and good.

en høvding.explanation: "En høvding" means "a chieftain". The word is also part of "en indianerhøvding" (a Native American chief).

sentence.da: Stammens **høvding** er den, der leder og beskytter sit folk.
sentence.en: The tribe's chieftain is the one who leads and protects his people.

et halvår.explanation: "Et halvår" means "a half year". It is built from "halv" (half) and "et år" (a year). To talk about one half of the calendar year, use "første halvår" (the first half of the year).

sentence.da: Vi har boet i Danmark i et **halvår**, altså seks måneder.
sentence.en: We have lived in Denmark for half a year, that is, six months.

et handicap.explanation: "Et handicap" means "a disability". The form "handicappet" also means "disabled": "Han er handicappet" (He is disabled). When it means "the disability", it is a noun: "Handicappet gør hverdagen svær" (The disability makes everyday life hard).

sentence.da: Rampen gør det nemmere for mennesker med et **handicap** at komme ind.
sentence.en: The ramp makes it easier for people with a disability to get in.

et hashtag.explanation: "Et hashtag" means "a hashtag". To talk about more than one, add "s": "Hun bruger mange hashtags" (She uses many hashtags).

sentence.da: Jeg satte et **hashtag** under mit billede.
sentence.en: I put a hashtag under my picture.

et hav.explanation: "Et hav" means "a sea". The word also ends the names of oceans, such as "Atlanterhavet" (the Atlantic Ocean). To say where you live, use "ved" (by): "Vi bor ved havet" (We live by the sea). The plural "have" is spelled like "en have" (a garden): "Vi sidder i haven" (We sit in the garden).

sentence.da: Skibet sejler over det store **hav**.
sentence.en: The ship sails across the big sea.

et havnebad.explanation: "Et havnebad" means "a harbor bath (outdoor pool)". It is built from "en havn" (a harbor) and "et bad" (a bath).

sentence.da: Om sommeren hopper børnene i vandet fra et **havnebad** midt i byen.
sentence.en: In the summer, the children jump into the water from a harbor bath in the middle of town.

et headset.explanation: "Et headset" means "a headset". To say you put it on, use "at tage på" (to put on): "Tag dit headset på" (Put your headset on). The plural has no ending: "to headset" (two headsets).

sentence.da: Jeg bruger mit **headset** til videomøder.
sentence.en: I use my headset for video meetings.

et hegn.explanation: "Et hegn" means "a fence". Do not mix it up with "en hæk" (a hedge): "Vi har en hæk i stedet for et hegn" (We have a hedge instead of a fence).

sentence.da: Hunden kan ikke komme over det høje **hegn**.
sentence.en: The dog cannot get over the tall fence.

et hensyn.explanation: "Et hensyn" means "a consideration". A very common phrase is "at tage hensyn til" (to take into account): "Hun tager altid hensyn til børnene" (She always considers the children).

sentence.da: Af **hensyn** til naboerne slukker vi musikken klokken ti.
sentence.en: Out of consideration for the neighbors, we turn the music off at ten.

et hindbær.explanation: "Et hindbær" means "a raspberry". The ending "bær" means "berry", as in "et tranebær" (a cranberry) and "et stikkelsbær" (a gooseberry).

sentence.da: Jeg laver rød marmelade af **hindbær**.
sentence.en: I make red jam from raspberries.

et hit.explanation: "Et hit" means "a hit". It is not used for hitting with your hand. To say someone hits a ball, use "at slå" (to hit): "Han slår bolden" (He hits the ball).

sentence.da: Den nye sang er et stort **hit** i Danmark.
sentence.en: The new song is a big hit in Denmark.

et hjem.explanation: "Et hjem" means "a home". To say you are at home, use "hjemme": "Jeg er hjemme" (I am at home). To say you are going home, use "hjem": "Jeg går hjem" (I am going home). Do not mix it up with "et hus" (a house): "Vi har købt et hus" (We have bought a house).

sentence.da: Min familie er mit **hjem**.
sentence.en: My family is my home.

et hjemland.explanation: "Et hjemland" means "a home country". It is built from "hjem" (home) and "et land" (a country). To say you go back there, use "at vende tilbage til" (to return to): "Hun vender tilbage til sit hjemland" (She returns to her home country).

sentence.da: Danmark er mit **hjemland**, men jeg bor i Norge.
sentence.en: Denmark is my home country, but I live in Norway.

et hjerte.explanation: "Et hjerte" means "a heart". In "hjerte", the "h" is silent, so the word starts with the sound of "y" in "yes". To say you mean something deeply, use: "med hele mit hjerte" (with all my heart).

sentence.da: Mit **hjerte** slår hurtigt.
sentence.en: My heart is beating fast.

et hjerteanfald.explanation: "Et hjerteanfald" means "a heart attack". In Denmark, you call 112 in an emergency: "Ring 112!" (Call 112!) Do not mix it up with "et hjertestop" (cardiac arrest): "Ved hjertestop holder hjertet op med at slå" (In a cardiac arrest, the heart stops beating).

sentence.da: Han fik et **hjerteanfald**, men ambulancen kom hurtigt og reddede ham.
sentence.en: He had a heart attack, but the ambulance came quickly and saved him.

et hjerteslag.explanation: "Et hjerteslag" means "a heartbeat". It is built from "et hjerte" (a heart) and "et slag" (a beat). To say how many beats you have in a minute, use "en puls" (a pulse): "Min puls er halvfjerds" (My pulse is seventy).

sentence.da: Lægen lytter efter patientens **hjerteslag** med et stetoskop.
sentence.en: The doctor listens for the patient's heartbeat with a stethoscope.

et hjertestop.explanation: "Et hjertestop" means "a cardiac arrest". It is built from "et hjerte" (a heart) and "et stop" (a stop). To say someone has one, use "at få" (to get): "Manden fik hjertestop" (The man had a cardiac arrest). Do not mix it up with "et hjerteanfald" (a heart attack): "Han fik et hjerteanfald" (He had a heart attack).

sentence.da: Ved **hjertestop** skal man straks ringe 112 og starte hjertemassage.
sentence.en: In a cardiac arrest, you must call 112 at once and start chest compressions.

et hjul.explanation: "Et hjul" means "a wheel". The word also builds "et cykelhjul" (a bicycle wheel). The plural has no ending: "to hjul" (two wheels).

sentence.da: Jeg skal skifte et **hjul** på bilen.
sentence.en: I have to change a wheel on the car.

et hjørne.explanation: "Et hjørne" means "a corner". To say where a shop is on the street, use "på hjørnet" (on the corner): "Bageren ligger på hjørnet" (The bakery is on the corner). To say where something is in a room, use "i hjørnet" (in the corner): "Stolen står i hjørnet" (The chair is in the corner).

sentence.da: Der er en lampe i hvert **hjørne** af rummet.
sentence.en: There is a lamp in every corner of the room.

et hjørnespark.explanation: "Et hjørnespark" means "a corner kick". It is built from "et hjørne" (a corner) and "et spark" (a kick). The part "spark" also builds "et straffespark" (a penalty kick).

sentence.da: Spilleren stiller bolden ved flaget og tager et **hjørnespark**.
sentence.en: The player puts the ball by the flag and takes a corner kick.

et hobbyrum.explanation: "Et hobbyrum" means "a hobby room". It is built from "en hobby" (a hobby) and "et rum" (a room). The part "rum" also builds "et lagerrum" (a storage room).

sentence.da: Min mand bygger modelskibe i et lille **hobbyrum**.
sentence.en: My husband builds model ships in a small hobby room.

et hold.explanation: "Et hold" means "a team". To say people work well together, use it for the group: "Vi er et godt hold" (We are a good team). When you sign up for lessons, it also means "a course group": "Jeg går på et hold om aftenen" (I take a course in the evening).

sentence.da: Vores **hold** vandt kampen i går.
sentence.en: Our team won the match yesterday.

et horn.explanation: "Et horn" means "a horn". When you mean the musical instrument, it is also "et horn": "Han blæser i et jagthorn" (He blows a hunting horn). A deer has "et gevir" (a set of antlers), not horns: "Hjorten har et stort gevir" (The deer has big antlers).

sentence.da: Både tyre og køer har **horn** på hovedet.
sentence.en: Both bulls and cows have horns on their heads.

et hospital.explanation: "Et hospital" means "a hospital". To say where you are, Danish uses "på" (on) where English says "at": "Jeg er på hospitalet" (I am at the hospital).

sentence.da: Lægen arbejder på et **hospital**.
sentence.en: The doctor works at a hospital.

et hotel.explanation: "Et hotel" means "a hotel". To say where you are staying, Danish uses "på" (on) where English says "at": "Vi bor på hotel" (We are staying at a hotel).

sentence.da: På et **hotel** kan man sove.
sentence.en: At a hotel you can sleep.

et hotelværelse.explanation: "Et hotelværelse" means "a hotel room". It is built from hotel (hotel) and værelse (room). To say you have a booking: "Jeg har bestilt et hotelværelse" (I have booked a hotel room).

sentence.da: Mit **hotelværelse** har udsigt til havnen.
sentence.en: My hotel room has a view of the harbor.

et hoved.explanation: "Et hoved" means "a head". To say your head hurts, Danish says "the head" where English says "my head": "Jeg har ondt i hovedet" (My head hurts, literally "I have a pain in the head"). In "hovedpine" (headache) it means the body part. In "hovedstad" (capital city) it means "main".

sentence.da: Hun har en stor hat på sit **hoved**.
sentence.en: She has a big hat on her head.

et hovedkvarter.explanation: "Et hovedkvarter" means "a headquarters". It is built from hoved (main) and et kvarter (a district).

sentence.da: Firmaets **hovedkvarter** ligger i København, men der er kontorer i hele landet.
sentence.en: The company's headquarters is in Copenhagen, but there are offices all over the country.

et hul.explanation: "Et hul" means "a hole". To say you have a cavity, use it with "tanden" (the tooth): "Jeg har et hul i tanden" (I have a cavity in my tooth).

sentence.da: Hunden graver et **hul** i haven.
sentence.en: The dog is digging a hole in the garden.

et humør.explanation: "Et humør" means "a mood". To say someone is in a bad mood, put "i" (in) before it: "Han er i dårligt humør" (He is in a bad mood).

sentence.da: Hun er i godt **humør** i dag.
sentence.en: She is in a good mood today.

et hundehalsbånd.explanation: "Et hundehalsbånd" means "a dog collar". It is built from hund (dog), hals (neck) and bånd (band).

sentence.da: Hunden har et nyt **hundehalsbånd** på.
sentence.en: The dog has a new dog collar on.

et hus.explanation: "Et hus" means "a house". Do not mix it up with "et hjem" (a home). To talk about the building you buy, use "et hus": "Vi køber et hus" (We are buying a house). To talk about where you belong, use "et hjem": "Jeg savner mit hjem" (I miss my home).

sentence.da: Et **hus** har vægge, et tag og vinduer.
sentence.en: A house has walls, a roof and windows.

et husdyr.explanation: "Et husdyr" means "a domestic animal". It is built from hus (house) and dyr (animal).

sentence.da: På gården har vi mange **husdyr**, som køer og høns.
sentence.en: On the farm we have many domestic animals, like cows and hens.

et husnummer.explanation: "Et husnummer" means "a house number". It is built from hus (house) and nummer (number). To write an address, put the number after the street name: "Nørregade 12" (Nørregade number 12).

sentence.da: Jeg kan ikke se dit **husnummer** på døren.
sentence.en: I cannot see your house number on the door.

et håndarbejde.explanation: "Et håndarbejde" means "a handicraft". It is built from hånd (hand) and arbejde (work). Do not mix it up with "et håndværk" (a skilled trade). To say someone works in a trade: "Min onkel er tømrer, og det er et håndværk" (My uncle is a carpenter, and that is a skilled trade).

sentence.da: Strikning og broderi er begge slags **håndarbejde**.
sentence.en: Knitting and embroidery are both kinds of handicraft.

et håndjern.explanation: "Et håndjern" means "a handcuff". It is built from hånd (hand) and jern (iron). To say someone is wearing handcuffs: "Han har håndjern på" (He has handcuffs on).

sentence.da: Politiet anholdt manden og tog **håndjern** på ham.
sentence.en: The police arrested the man and put handcuffs on him.

et håndklæde.explanation: "Et håndklæde" means "a towel". Do not mix it up with "et viskestykke" (a dish towel). To dry a dish, use "et viskestykke": "Jeg tørrer glasset med et viskestykke" (I dry the glass with a dish towel).

sentence.da: Efter badet tørrer jeg mig med et **håndklæde**.
sentence.en: After the bath, I dry myself with a towel.

et håndled.explanation: "Et håndled" means "a wrist". It is built from en hånd (a hand) and et led (a joint). To say your wrist hurts: "Jeg har ondt i håndleddet" (My wrist hurts).

sentence.da: Han har et ur om sit **håndled**.
sentence.en: He has a watch around his wrist.

et håndtag.explanation: "Et håndtag" means "a handle". It is built from en hånd (a hand) and et tag (a hold), so it is what you take hold of.

sentence.da: Skuffen går ikke op, fordi dens **håndtag** er gået i stykker.
sentence.en: The drawer will not open, because its handle is broken.

et håndtryk.explanation: "Et håndtryk" means "a handshake". It is built from hånd (hand) and et tryk (a press). To say two people shake hands, use "at give hånd" (to shake hands): "Vi giver hinanden hånd" (We shake hands).

sentence.da: Aftalen blev sluttet med et fast **håndtryk**.
sentence.en: The deal was sealed with a firm handshake.

et håndværk.explanation: "Et håndværk" means "a craft". It is built from hånd (hand) and et værk (a work). Do not mix it up with "et håndarbejde" (a handicraft). To say what knitting is: "Hun strikker, og det er et håndarbejde" (She knits, and that is a handicraft).

sentence.da: Det tager flere år at lære et **håndværk**, for eksempel som tømrer.
sentence.en: It takes several years to learn a craft, for example as a carpenter.

et hårspænde.explanation: "Et hårspænde" means "a hair clip". It is built from hår (hair) and et spænde (a clasp).

sentence.da: Hun har et lille **hårspænde** i håret.
sentence.en: She has a small hair clip in her hair.

et hæfte.explanation: "Et hæfte" means "a notebook". When you mean a thin booklet that comes with something, it is also "et hæfte": "et hæfte med opskrifter" (a booklet of recipes).

sentence.da: Jeg skriver mine lektier i mit **hæfte**.
sentence.en: I write my homework in my notebook.

et højhus.explanation: "Et højhus" means "a high-rise". It is built from høj (tall) and hus (house).

sentence.da: Hun bor meget højt oppe i et **højhus**.
sentence.en: She lives very high up in a high-rise.

et højskoleophold.explanation: "Et højskoleophold" means "a folk high school stay". It is built from "en højskole" (a folk high school) and "et ophold" (a stay). Folk high schools began in Denmark as schools where adults live and study together.

sentence.da: På et **højskoleophold** bor man på skolen og lærer noget sammen med andre.
sentence.en: On a folk high school stay, you live at the school and learn something together with others.

et høreapparat.explanation: "Et høreapparat" means "a hearing aid". It is built from høre (hear) and et apparat (a device).

sentence.da: Min bedstefar har fået et **høreapparat**, så han kan høre fjernsynet.
sentence.en: My grandfather has gotten a hearing aid, so he can hear the TV.

had.explanation: "Had" means "a hatred". It is the noun for the verb "at hade" (to hate). To say who the hatred is aimed at, add "mod" (toward): "Hun følte had mod ham" (She felt hatred toward him).

sentence.da: Der var **had** i hans stemme.
sentence.en: There was hatred in his voice.

hagl.explanation: "Hagl" means "hail". When you mean the small lead pellets fired from a shotgun, it is also "hagl": "Jægeren lader sit haglgevær med hagl" (The hunter loads his shotgun with pellets).

sentence.da: Store **hagl** faldt og ødelagde ruden på bilen.
sentence.en: Large hail fell and broke the window of the car.

hakket oksekød.explanation: "Hakket oksekød" means "ground beef". It is built from hakket (chopped) and oksekød (beef). To say ground pork, swap the meat: "hakket svinekød" (ground pork).

sentence.da: Vi bruger **hakket oksekød** til lasagne.
sentence.en: We use ground beef for lasagna.

hallo.explanation: "Hallo" means "hello". To get someone's attention, say it sharply: "Hallo, hører du efter?" (Hello, are you listening?).

sentence.da: Telefonen ringer. **Hallo**, hvem er det?
sentence.en: The phone rings. Hello, who is it?

halløj.explanation: "Halløj" means "hey". It is an informal greeting. To greet a friend and ask how things are: "Halløj, hvad så?" (Hey, what is up?).

sentence.da: **Halløj**, har I det godt?
sentence.en: Hey, are you all doing well?

halm.explanation: "Halm" means "straw". Do not mix it up with "et sugerør" (a drinking straw). To say you drink through a straw: "Jeg drikker med et sugerør" (I drink with a drinking straw).

sentence.da: Taget på det gamle hus er lavet af **halm**.
sentence.en: The roof of the old house is made of straw.

halv.explanation: "Halv" means "half". It goes before the word it describes: "en halv liter" (half a liter). To say half past the hour on the clock, count toward the next hour: "klokken fire" (four o'clock) is 4:00, but "halv fire" is 3:30, half an hour before four.

sentence.da: En **halv** time er tredive minutter.
sentence.en: Half an hour is thirty minutes.

halv tre.explanation: "Halv tre" means "half past two". Danish counts halfway toward the next hour, so 2:30 is "halv tre" (halfway to three).

forms.en: See you at half past six.

sentence.da: Det er **halv tre**, tredive minutter før tre.
sentence.en: It is half past two, thirty minutes before three.

halvanden.explanation: "Halvanden" means "one and a half". To say an hour and a half, put it before "time" (hour): "halvanden time". Before "år" (year) it changes to "halvandet": "halvandet år" (a year and a half).

sentence.da: Jeg venter i **halvanden** time.
sentence.en: I am waiting for an hour and a half.

halvdelen.explanation: "Halvdelen" means "a half". To name the whole that the half comes from, add "af" (of): "halvdelen af pengene" (half of the money). For a measure such as half a liter, use "halv" (half): "en halv liter" (half a liter).

sentence.da: Jeg har spist **halvdelen** af kagen.
sentence.en: I have eaten half of the cake.

halvfems.explanation: "Halvfems" means "ninety". It is short for "halvfemsindstyve": halfway to five twenties (4½ x 20 = 90). For 91, you say "enoghalvfems" (literally, "one-and-ninety").

sentence.da: Min bedstefar er **halvfems** år og snart hundrede.
sentence.en: My grandfather is ninety years old and will soon be a hundred.

halvfjerds.explanation: "Halvfjerds" means "seventy". Danes count it as halfway to four twenties (3½ x 20 = 70). For 71, you say "enoghalvfjerds" (literally, "one-and-seventy").

sentence.da: **Halvfjerds** er ti mere end tres.
sentence.en: Seventy is ten more than sixty.

halvtreds.explanation: "Halvtreds" means "fifty". Danes count it as halfway to three twenties (2½ x 20 = 50). For 51, you say "enoghalvtreds" (literally, "one-and-fifty").

sentence.da: **Halvtreds** er det halve af hundrede.
sentence.en: Fifty is half of a hundred.

halvvejs.explanation: "Halvvejs" means "halfway". It is built from halv (half) and vej (way). To talk about time: "halvvejs gennem året" (halfway through the year).

sentence.da: Vi har kørt i to timer og er nu **halvvejs**.
sentence.en: We have driven for two hours and are now halfway.

ham.explanation: "Ham" means "him". When a man receives the action, use "ham": "Jeg hjælper ham" (I help him). When the man does the action, use "han" (he): "Han hjælper mig" (He helps me). After "med" (with) it is also "ham": "Jeg går med ham" (I am going with him).

sentence.da: Peter er min ven. Jeg kan lide **ham**.
sentence.en: Peter is my friend. I like him.

han.explanation: "Han" means "he". When a man does the action, use "han": "Han hjælper mig" (He helps me). When the man receives the action, use "ham" (him): "Jeg hjælper ham" (I help him).

sentence.da: **Han** er min bror.
sentence.en: He is my brother.

handsker.explanation: "Handsker" means "gloves". Do not mix it up with "en vante" (a mitten). To say children wear mittens: "Børnene har røde vanter på" (The children have red mittens on).

sentence.da: Om vinteren har jeg **handsker** på hænderne.
sentence.en: In winter I wear gloves on my hands.

hans.explanation: "Hans" means "his". When the owner is a man other than the one doing the action, use "hans": "Peter vasker hans bil" (Peter washes another man's car). To say the man's own, use "sin": "Peter vasker sin bil" (Peter washes his own car).

sentence.da: Peter har en hund. **Hans** hund er stor.
sentence.en: Peter has a dog. His dog is big.

hardware.explanation: "Hardware" means "hardware". Danish took this word from English and spells it the same way.

sentence.da: Min computer er gammel, så jeg køber ny **hardware**.
sentence.en: My computer is old, so I am buying new hardware.

hav en god dag.explanation: "Hav en god dag" means "have a good day". To say it as a goodbye and get a reply: "Hav en god dag!" "Tak, i lige måde." (Have a good day! Thanks, you too.) To wish someone a good evening, swap "dag" (day) for "aften" (evening): "Hav en god aften" (Have a good evening).

sentence.da: Tak for hjælpen. **Hav en god dag**!
sentence.en: Thanks for the help. Have a good day!

havearbejde.explanation: "Havearbejde" means "gardening". It is built from have (garden) and arbejde (work). To say you do it, use "at lave" (to make): "Jeg laver havearbejde" (I do gardening).

sentence.da: **Havearbejde** er at plante blomster og klippe græs.
sentence.en: Gardening is planting flowers and cutting grass.

havre.explanation: "Havre" means "oats". In "havregryn" (rolled oats) and "havremælk" (oat milk), "havre" is the first part of the word.

sentence.da: Jeg spiser grød med **havre** hver morgen.
sentence.en: I eat porridge with oats every morning.

havregryn.explanation: "Havregryn" means "oatmeal". It is built from havre (oats) and gryn (groats). To name the cooked porridge, say "havregrød" (oatmeal porridge): "Jeg laver havregrød" (I am making oatmeal porridge).

forms.en: We have oatmeal in the cupboard.

sentence.da: Jeg spiser **havregryn** med mælk og banan.
sentence.en: I eat oatmeal with milk and banana.

havremælk.explanation: "Havremælk" means "oat milk". It is built from havre (oats) and mælk (milk).

sentence.da: **Havremælk** er en drik lavet af havre.
sentence.en: Oat milk is a drink made from oats.

hed.explanation: "Hed" means "hot". Do not mix it up with "varm" (warm), which is milder: "Vandet er varmt" (The water is warm). When the thing described takes "et", add "t": "et hedt bad" (a hot bath).

sentence.da: Kaffen er så **hed**, at jeg brænder mig på tungen.
sentence.en: The coffee is so hot that I burn my tongue.

hej.explanation: "Hej" means "hi". To say goodbye, say it twice: "Hej hej!" (Bye bye!).

sentence.da: **Hej**, jeg hedder Anna.
sentence.en: Hi, my name is Anna.

hej med dig.explanation: "Hej med dig" means "hi there". When you leave, it also means "bye": "Hej med dig, vi ses!" (Bye, see you!). To greet several people, say "hej med jer" (hi to you all): "Hej med jer!" (Hi to you all!).

sentence.da: **Hej med dig**, Anna!
sentence.en: Hi there, Anna!

hejsa.explanation: "Hejsa" means "hi there". It is an informal, cheerful version of "hej" (hi). To greet someone and ask how they are: "Hejsa, hvordan har du det?" (Hi there, how are you?).

sentence.da: **Hejsa**, Peter!
sentence.en: Hi there, Peter!

hektisk.explanation: "Hektisk" means "hectic". Before a word that takes "et", it does not add "t": "et hektisk liv" (a hectic life). With several things, it adds "e": "hektiske tider" (hectic times).

sentence.da: Det var en **hektisk** dag med møder fra morgen til aften.
sentence.en: It was a hectic day with meetings from morning to evening.

hel.explanation: "Hel" means "whole". To say a whole thing, put it before the noun: "en hel kage" (a whole cake). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et helt æble" (a whole apple). To say "the whole day", use "hele": "hele dagen" (the whole day). When something is not broken, it also means "unbroken": "Koppen er hel" (The cup is unbroken).

sentence.da: Jeg spiste en **hel** pizza og ikke bare et stykke.
sentence.en: I ate a whole pizza and not just a slice.

helbred.explanation: "Helbred" means "health". To say someone's health is poor, put "dårligt" (poor) before it: "Han har dårligt helbred" (He has poor health). Do not mix it up with "sund" (healthy), which describes food: "sund mad" (healthy food).

sentence.da: Min bedstefar har et godt **helbred**.
sentence.en: My grandfather has good health.

held.explanation: "Held" means "luck". It is the first word in the phrase "held og lykke" (good luck): "Held og lykke med eksamen" (Good luck with the exam).

sentence.da: Jeg havde **held** og fandt en ledig plads.
sentence.en: I got lucky and found a free seat.

held og lykke.explanation: "Held og lykke" means "good luck" (literally, "luck and happiness"). To name the event or task you wish the person luck with, add "med" (with) after it: "held og lykke med prøven" (good luck with the test).

sentence.da: **Held og lykke** med dit nye job!
sentence.en: Good luck with your new job!

heldig.explanation: "Heldig" means "lucky". It comes from "held" (luck), as does "heldigvis" (fortunately). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et heldigt valg" (a lucky choice).

sentence.da: Jeg var **heldig** og vandt en bil.
sentence.en: I was lucky and won a car.

heldigvis.explanation: "Heldigvis" means "fortunately". To say you are glad about how something turned out: "Heldigvis er det fredag" (Fortunately it is Friday). The opposite is "desværre" (unfortunately): "Desværre har jeg ikke tid" (Unfortunately I do not have time).

sentence.da: **Heldigvis** havde jeg en paraply med.
sentence.en: Fortunately I had an umbrella with me.

hele tiden.explanation: "Hele tiden" means "all the time". Literally, it is "the whole time". To say "always", use "altid" (always): "Han kommer altid til tiden" (He always arrives on time).

sentence.da: Hun ringer **hele tiden**.
sentence.en: She calls all the time.

heller.explanation: "Heller" means "either", as in "not either". To say yes to the same thing, use "også" (too): "Jeg kan også komme" (I can come too). To say no, use "heller ikke": "Jeg kan heller ikke komme" (I cannot come either).

sentence.da: Han kommer ikke, og jeg kommer **heller** ikke.
sentence.en: He is not coming, and I am not coming either.

hellere.explanation: "Hellere" means "rather". With "må" (must) it means "had better": "Du må hellere gå nu" (You had better go now). Do not mix it up with "heller" (either): "Jeg kan heller ikke komme" (I cannot come either).

forms.da: hellere i dag end i morgen

sentence.da: Jeg vil **hellere** gå end tage bussen.
sentence.en: I would rather walk than take the bus.

hellere end.explanation: "Hellere end" means "rather than". To say which choice you take and which you skip, name the one you take first: "Jeg tager toget hellere end bilen" (I take the train rather than the car). To say "better late than never": "Hellere sent end aldrig" (literally, "rather late than never").

sentence.da: Jeg vil blive hjemme **hellere end** at gå ud.
sentence.en: I would rather stay home than go out.

hellig.explanation: "Hellig" means "sacred". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et helligt sted" (a holy place). It is also the first part of "helligdag" (public holiday), literally "holy day".

sentence.da: Kirken er **hellig** for de troende.
sentence.en: The church is holy to the believers.

helst.explanation: "Helst" means "preferably". To say what you would like most: "Jeg vil helst blive hjemme" (I would most like to stay home). To say you would rather not: "Skal du med?" "Helst ikke." (Are you coming? Preferably not.)

sentence.da: Jeg vil **helst** bo ved havet.
sentence.en: I would most like to live by the sea.

helt.explanation: "Helt" means "completely". To say something is complete, put it before the word: "Jeg er enig" (I agree) becomes "Jeg er helt enig" (I completely agree).

sentence.da: Glasset er **helt** tomt.
sentence.en: The glass is completely empty.

hemmelig.explanation: "Hemmelig" means "secret". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hemmeligt sted" (a secret place). The noun is "en hemmelighed" (a secret): "Det er en hemmelighed" (It is a secret).

sentence.da: Vi har en **hemmelig** plan til din fødselsdag.
sentence.en: We have a secret plan for your birthday.

hemmelighedsfuld.explanation: "Hemmelighedsfuld" means "secretive". It is built from "en hemmelighed" (a secret) and "-fuld" (full of). The ending "-fuld" also appears in "hensynsfuld" (considerate). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hemmelighedsfuldt smil" (a secretive smile).

sentence.da: Hun er **hemmelighedsfuld** og fortæller aldrig noget om sig selv.
sentence.en: She is secretive and never tells anything about herself.

hen.explanation: "Hen" means "over", as in moving over to a place. When someone moves to a place, use it with the verb: "Gå hen til døren" (Walk over to the door). For where someone already is, use "henne" (over there): "Han står henne ved døren" (He stands over there by the door).

sentence.da: Hun går **hen** til sin ven og siger hej.
sentence.en: She walks over to her friend and says hi.

hende.explanation: "Hende" means "her". When a woman receives the action, use "hende": "Jeg hjælper hende" (I help her). When the woman does the action, use "hun" (she): "Hun hjælper mig" (She helps me). After "med" (with) it is also "hende": "Jeg går med hende" (I am going with her).

sentence.da: Anna er min ven. Jeg kan lide **hende**.
sentence.en: Anna is my friend. I like her.

hendes.explanation: "Hendes" means "her". When the owner is a woman other than the one doing the action, use "hendes": "Anna vasker hendes bil" (Anna washes another woman's car). To say the woman's own, use "sin": "Anna vasker sin bil" (Anna washes her own car).

sentence.da: Bilen er **hendes**, ikke min.
sentence.en: The car is hers, not mine.

hensynsfuld.explanation: "Hensynsfuld" means "considerate". It is built from "et hensyn" (a consideration) and "-fuld" (full of). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hensynsfuldt svar" (a considerate answer).

sentence.da: Han er **hensynsfuld** og går stille forbi, når babyen sover.
sentence.en: He is considerate and walks past quietly when the baby is sleeping.

her.explanation: "Her" means "here". To say where you are: "Jeg står her" (I am standing here). For a place away from you, use "der" (there): "Du står der" (You are standing there). Do not mix it up with the English word "her", which is "hende" in Danish: "Jeg ser hende" (I see her).

sentence.da: Jeg bor **her** i huset.
sentence.en: I live here in the house.

herfra.explanation: "Herfra" means "from here". It is built from her (here) and fra (from). For a place away from you, use "derfra" (from there): "Det er langt derfra" (It is far from there).

forms.en: From here you can see the town

sentence.da: **Herfra** er der kun fem minutter til stationen.
sentence.en: From here it is only five minutes to the station.

herhen.explanation: "Herhen" means "here", when someone moves toward the speaker. To say someone walks toward the speaker: "Hun går herhen" (She walks here). To say where someone already is, use "her" (here): "Jeg er her" (I am here).

sentence.da: Kan du komme **herhen** et øjeblik?
sentence.en: Can you come here for a moment?

herinde.explanation: "Herinde" means "in here". It is built from her (here) and inde (inside). When someone outside says where a person is, use "derinde" (in there): "Hun er derinde" (She is in there).

sentence.da: Jeg er **herinde**, ikke udenfor.
sentence.en: I am in here, not outside.

herlig.explanation: "Herlig" means "wonderful". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et herligt vejr" (lovely weather). With several things, it adds "e": "herlige børn" (lovely children).

sentence.da: Solen skinner, og dagen er **herlig**.
sentence.en: The sun is shining, and the day is wonderful.

hermed.explanation: "Hermed" means "hereby". It is built from her (here) and med (with). It is a formal word. To announce that something is now official: "Hermed erklæres mødet for åbnet" (The meeting is hereby declared open).

forms.en: The meeting is hereby declared open
I hereby send you the contract

sentence.da: **Hermed** sender jeg dig regningen og et par billeder.
sentence.en: I hereby send you the bill and a few pictures.

hertil.explanation: "Hertil" means "here", when someone moves toward the place. To add one more thing to what you just said: "Hertil kommer prisen" (On top of this comes the price).

sentence.da: Vi tog toget **hertil** i går.
sentence.en: We took the train here yesterday.

herude.explanation: "Herude" means "out here". It is built from her (here) and ude (out). For a place away from you, use "derude" (out there): "Det er koldt derude" (It is cold out there).

sentence.da: Jeg fryser, når jeg står **herude** uden jakke.
sentence.en: I freeze when I stand out here without a jacket.

hidsig.explanation: "Hidsig" means "hot-tempered". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hidsigt temperament" (a hot temper). With several people, it adds "e": "hidsige drenge" (hot-tempered boys).

sentence.da: Han er **hidsig** og råber af folk for små ting.
sentence.en: He is hot-tempered and shouts at people over small things.

hidtil.explanation: "Hidtil" means "so far". To say things go on as before: "Vi gør det som hidtil" (We do it as before). For a set end point, use "indtil" (until): "Jeg bliver indtil fredag" (I am staying until Friday).

forms.en: So far it has gone well

sentence.da: **Hidtil** har jeg kun boet i Danmark.
sentence.en: So far, I have only lived in Denmark.

hinanden.explanation: "Hinanden" means "each other". To say people do the same thing to one another: "De vasker hinanden" (They wash each other). To say each person does it to themselves, use "sig" (themselves): "De vasker sig" (They wash themselves).

sentence.da: Min mor og far elsker **hinanden**.
sentence.en: My mom and dad love each other.

hinsides.explanation: "Hinsides" means "beyond", as in on the far side of a place: "hinsides floden" (beyond the river). To say something is past a limit, it also means "beyond": "hinsides enhver tvivl" (beyond any doubt).

sentence.da: Vi skal over broen, fordi byen ligger **hinsides** floden.
sentence.en: We have to cross the bridge because the town lies beyond the river.

historisk.explanation: "Historisk" means "historic". To say something is about the past, it means "historical": "en historisk roman" (a historical novel).

sentence.da: Det var en **historisk** aften for hele landet.
sentence.en: It was a historic evening for the whole country.

hittegods.explanation: "Hittegods" means "lost and found". It is built from "at hitte" (to find) and "gods" (goods). To say where you ask for lost things: "Hittegodset er åbent i dag" (The lost and found is open today).

forms.en: I am looking for the lost and found
We hand it in as lost-and-found items
It is in the lost and found

sentence.da: Har I **hittegods**? Jeg har mistet min jakke.
sentence.en: Do you have a lost and found? I lost my jacket.

hjem.explanation: "Hjem" means "home". When you are heading there, use it with a verb of moving: "Jeg går hjem" (I am going home). When you are already there, use "hjemme" (at home): "Jeg er hjemme" (I am at home).

sentence.da: Jeg skal **hjem** nu.
sentence.en: I am going home now.

hjemlig.explanation: "Hjemlig" means "homey". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hjemligt køkken" (a homey kitchen). When you mean from your own country, it means "domestic": "hjemlige produkter" (domestic products).

sentence.da: Caféen har en **hjemlig** stemning med bløde stole og levende lys.
sentence.en: The café has a homey atmosphere with soft chairs and candles.

hjemløs.explanation: "Hjemløs" means "homeless". It is built from hjem (home) and the ending -løs (without). To talk about the people, use it as a noun: "de hjemløse" (the homeless).

sentence.da: Manden er **hjemløs** og sover på gaden om natten.
sentence.en: The man is homeless and sleeps on the street at night.

hjemme.explanation: "Hjemme" means "at home", where you already are: "Jeg er hjemme" (I am at home). When you are heading there, use "hjem" (home): "Jeg går hjem" (I am going home). To say at someone's place, add "hos" (at): "hjemme hos mig" (at my place).

sentence.da: Jeg er **hjemme** i aften.
sentence.en: I am at home tonight.

hjemmelavet.explanation: "Hjemmelavet" means "homemade". It is built from hjemme (at home) and lavet (made). The word "lavet" (made) is also in "håndlavet" (handmade).

sentence.da: Kagen er **hjemmelavet**, ikke købt i butikken.
sentence.en: The cake is homemade, not bought in the store.

hjælp.explanation: "Hjælp" means "help". It takes "en" (hjælpen), but to ask for help in general, leave it out: "Kan jeg få hjælp?" (Can I get help?) To thank someone: "Tak for hjælpen" (Thanks for the help).

sentence.da: Jeg har brug for **hjælp**!
sentence.en: I need help!

hjælpeløs.explanation: "Hjælpeløs" means "helpless". It is built from hjælp (help) and the ending -løs (without). To say how you feel: "Jeg følte mig hjælpeløs" (I felt helpless). Do not confuse it with "hjælpsom" (helpful): "en hjælpsom nabo" (a helpful neighbor).

sentence.da: En nyfødt baby er **hjælpeløs** og har brug for sine forældre.
sentence.en: A newborn baby is helpless and needs its parents.

hjælpsom.explanation: "Hjælpsom" means "helpful". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hjælpsomt barn" (a helpful child). Do not mix it up with "hjælpeløs" (helpless): "en hjælpeløs baby" (a helpless baby).

sentence.da: Min nabo er **hjælpsom** og bærer mine poser.
sentence.en: My neighbor is helpful and carries my bags.

hjælpsomhed.explanation: "Hjælpsomhed" means "helpfulness". It is built from "hjælpsom" (helpful) and the ending -hed (-ness). To thank someone: "Tak for din hjælpsomhed" (Thanks for your helpfulness).

sentence.da: Alle roser hans **hjælpsomhed**, fordi han altid hjælper sine naboer.
sentence.en: Everyone praises his helpfulness because he always helps his neighbors.

hold da op.explanation: "Hold da op" means "wow". To react to something impressive: "Hold da op, hvor flot!" (Wow, how pretty!) Do not mix it up with "hold op" (stop it): "Hold op med det!" (Stop that!).

sentence.da: **Hold da op**, hvor er den bil hurtig!
sentence.en: Wow, that car is fast!

hold kæft.explanation: "Hold kæft" means "shut up". It is rude. When you are very surprised, it can also mean "wow": "Hold kæft, hvor er det flot!" (Wow, that is so pretty!)

forms.da: Hold kæft, hvor er det flot!

sentence.da: **Hold kæft**, jeg troede ikke, du ville komme!
sentence.en: Wow, I did not think you would come!

hold op.explanation: "Hold op" means "stop it". To say you stop doing something, add "med at" (literally, "with to") before the verb: "Jeg holder op med at ryge" (I am quitting smoking).

sentence.da: **Hold op** med at drille mig!
sentence.en: Stop teasing me!

holdbar.explanation: "Holdbar" means "lasting". When you talk about a material, it means "durable": "et holdbart materiale" (a durable material). It is also the first part of "holdbarhedsdato" (best-before date).

sentence.da: Cyklen er **holdbar** og kan klare mange års brug.
sentence.en: The bike is durable and can handle many years of use.

holland.explanation: "Holland" means "the Netherlands". Danish has no word for "the" before it: "Jeg bor i Holland" (I live in the Netherlands).

sentence.da: I **Holland** taler de hollandsk.
sentence.en: In the Netherlands they speak Dutch.

hollandsk.explanation: "Hollandsk" means "Dutch". It comes from "Holland" (the Netherlands). To say what language you speak, put it after "taler" (speak): "Jeg taler hollandsk" (I speak Dutch).

sentence.da: Han bor i Holland og taler **hollandsk**.
sentence.en: He lives in the Netherlands and speaks Dutch.

honning.explanation: "Honning" means "honey". To say what is on your bread, use "på" (on): "Jeg har honning på brødet" (I have honey on my bread).

sentence.da: Bier laver **honning** af blomster.
sentence.en: Bees make honey from flowers.

hos.explanation: "Hos" means "at". When you say you are at a person's home or practice, put the person after it: "hos min ven" (at my friend's place) and "hos lægen" (at the doctor's). To say you are at a building, use "på" (at) instead: "Jeg er på biblioteket" (I am at the library).

sentence.da: Jeg sover **hos** min ven i nat.
sentence.en: I am sleeping at my friend's place tonight.

hovedsagelig.explanation: "Hovedsagelig" means "mainly". The start "hoved" means "main" in other words, such as "hovedgade" (main street).

sentence.da: Jeg læser **hovedsagelig** krimier, men nogle gange også biografier.
sentence.en: I mainly read crime novels, but sometimes also biographies.

hovedsageligt.explanation: "Hovedsageligt" means "mainly". The start "hoved" means "main" in other words, such as "hovedgade" (main street).

sentence.da: Flyet var **hovedsageligt** fyldt med turister, men også nogle forretningsfolk.
sentence.en: The plane was mainly full of tourists, but also some business people.

hud.explanation: "Hud" means "skin". It takes "en": "en hud". To say your skin is dry, use "tør" (dry): "Jeg har tør hud" (I have dry skin).

sentence.da: Solen kan brænde din **hud**.
sentence.en: The sun can burn your skin.

humor.explanation: "Humor" means "humor". To say someone has a sense of humor, use "sans" (sense) with "for" (for): "Hun har sans for humor" (She has a sense of humor).

sentence.da: Hun fortæller vittigheder og har god **humor**.
sentence.en: She tells jokes and has a good sense of humor.

humoristisk.explanation: "Humoristisk" means "humorous". It comes from "humor" (humor). To say something was fun, use "sjov" (fun) instead: "Det var sjovt!" (That was fun!)

sentence.da: Hans tale var **humoristisk**, og hele salen grinede.
sentence.en: His speech was humorous, and the whole room laughed.

hun.explanation: "Hun" means "she". When she does the action, use "hun": "Hun hjælper mig" (She helps me). When she receives the action, use "hende" (her): "Jeg hjælper hende" (I help her).

sentence.da: **Hun** er min søster.
sentence.en: She is my sister.

hundemad.explanation: "Hundemad" means "dog food". It is built from "hund" (dog) and "mad" (food). The word "mad" also ends "morgenmad" (breakfast) and "aftensmad" (dinner).

sentence.da: Hunden får **hundemad** to gange om dagen.
sentence.en: The dog gets dog food twice a day.

hundrede.explanation: "Hundrede" means "hundred". To say 200 or 300, put the number first and keep "hundrede" the same: "to hundrede" (200) and "tre hundrede" (300). To say 100, just say "hundrede"; no "en" (one) is needed.

sentence.da: Ti gange ti er **hundrede**.
sentence.en: Ten times ten is a hundred.

hundrededel.explanation: "Hundrededel" means "a hundredth". It is built from "hundrede" (hundred) and "del" (part). To say a tenth, use the same pattern: "en tiendedel" (a tenth).

sentence.da: Han vandt løbet med kun en **hundrededel** af et sekund.
sentence.en: He won the race by only a hundredth of a second.

hurra.explanation: "Hurra" means "hooray". To cheer together, say "hip hip hurra" (hip hip hooray).

sentence.da: **Hurra**, vi har fri i dag!
sentence.en: Hooray, we have the day off today!

hurtig.explanation: "Hurtig" means "fast". To say how someone does an action, use "hurtigt" (fast) instead: "Han løber hurtigt" (He runs fast).

sentence.da: Racerbilen er meget **hurtig**.
sentence.en: The race car is very fast.

husarbejde.explanation: "Husarbejde" means "housework". It is built from "hus" (house) and "arbejde" (work). To say you have a new job, use "arbejde" alone: "Jeg har et nyt arbejde" (I have a new job).

sentence.da: Jeg hader **husarbejde**, men jeg gør rent hver lørdag.
sentence.en: I hate housework, but I clean every Saturday.

husholdningsfilm.explanation: "Husholdningsfilm" means "plastic wrap". It is built from "husholdning" (household) and "film". Here "film" means a thin sheet, not a movie.

sentence.da: Jeg dækker skålen med **husholdningsfilm** og sætter den i køleskabet.
sentence.en: I cover the bowl with plastic wrap and put it in the refrigerator.

husleje.explanation: "Husleje" means "rent". It is built from "hus" (house) and "leje" (hire). To say you rent a car, use the verb "at leje" (to rent): "Jeg vil gerne leje en bil" (I would like to rent a car).

sentence.da: Jeg betaler **husleje** den første hver måned.
sentence.en: I pay rent on the first of every month.

hvabehar.explanation: "Hvabehar" means "pardon". It comes from "hvad behager", which literally means "what pleases". To show surprise, say it sharply: "Hvabehar! Er det sandt?" (What! Is it true?)

sentence.da: **Hvabehar**? Kan du sige det igen?
sentence.en: Pardon? Can you say it again?

hvad.explanation: "Hvad" means "what". To ask about a thing, use "hvad": "Hvad er det?" (What is that?). To ask about a person, use "hvem" (who) instead: "Hvem er det?" (Who is that?). When you did not hear something, "Hvad?" (What?) is blunt. "Undskyld?" (Excuse me?) is more polite.

sentence.da: **Hvad** hedder du?
sentence.en: What is your name?

hvad betyder det?.explanation: "Hvad betyder det?" means "What does that mean?". It is built from "hvad" (what), "betyder" (means) and "det" (that).

sentence.da: Jeg forstår ikke ordet. **Hvad betyder det?**
sentence.en: I don't understand the word. What does that mean?

hvad er klokken?.explanation: "Hvad er klokken?" means "What time is it?". Literally, it asks "what is the clock", because "klokken" means "the clock".

sentence.da: Undskyld, **hvad er klokken?**
sentence.en: Excuse me, what time is it?

hvad hedder det på dansk?.explanation: "Hvad hedder det på dansk?" means "What is that called in Danish?". The verb "hedder" (is called) is also used for names. To say your own name, say: "Jeg hedder Anna" (My name is Anna).

forms.en: What is that called in Danish?
What is that called in English?

sentence.da: Undskyld, **hvad hedder det på dansk?**
sentence.en: Excuse me, what is that called in Danish?

hvad hedder du?.explanation: "Hvad hedder du?" means "What's your name?". Literally, it asks what you are called. The verb in it is "hedder" (are called).

sentence.da: **Hvad hedder du?** - Jeg hedder Anna.
sentence.en: What's your name? - My name is Anna.

hvad koster det?.explanation: "Hvad koster det?" means "How much does it cost?". To ask about something that takes "et", such as "et hus" (a house), use "det" (it): "Hvad koster det?" To ask about something that takes "en", such as "en bog" (a book), use "den" (it): "Hvad koster den?" (How much does it cost?) To ask about several things, use "de" (they): "Hvad koster de?" (How much do they cost?)

sentence.da: **Hvad koster det?** Jeg vil gerne købe det.
sentence.en: How much does it cost? I'd like to buy it.

hvad laver du?.explanation: "Hvad laver du?" means "What are you doing?". To ask about someone's work, say "Hvad arbejder du med?" (What do you work with?). To ask several people, use "I" (you all): "Hvad laver I?" (What are you all doing?)

forms.en: What are you doing on the weekend?

related.en: what are you going to do?

sentence.da: **Hvad laver du** i aften?
sentence.en: What are you doing tonight?

hvad med dig?.explanation: "Hvad med dig?" means "What about you?". Literally, it is "what with you". To ask about a person by name, put the name in place of "dig" (you): "Hvad med Anna?" (What about Anna?)

sentence.da: Jeg har det godt. **Hvad med dig?**
sentence.en: I'm doing well. What about you?

hvad som helst.explanation: "Hvad som helst" means "anything". To say any person, use "hvem som helst" (anyone) instead: "Hvem som helst kan komme" (Anyone can come).

forms.da: Du kan vælge hvad som helst.

sentence.da: Jeg er sulten og spiser **hvad som helst**.
sentence.en: I am hungry and will eat anything.

hvad så?.explanation: "Hvad så?" means "What's up?". Literally, it is "what then", because "så" means "then" here. The same "så" means "so" in other places: "Jeg er så glad" (I am so happy).

sentence.da: Hej Anna, **hvad så?**
sentence.en: Hi Anna, what's up?

hvede.explanation: "Hvede" means "wheat". It also starts other words, such as "hvedebrød" (wheat bread) and "hvedemel" (wheat flour).

sentence.da: Af **hvede** laver man mel, og af mel bager man brød.
sentence.en: From wheat you make flour, and from flour you bake bread.

hvedemel.explanation: "Hvedemel" means "wheat flour". It is built from "hvede" (wheat) and "mel" (flour). Another word that starts with "hvede" is "hvedebrød" (wheat bread).

sentence.da: Jeg bager boller med **hvedemel** og vand.
sentence.en: I bake buns with wheat flour and water.

hvem.explanation: "Hvem" means "who". English has two forms, "who" and "whom", but Danish uses "hvem" for both. When it asks who does the action, say: "Hvem taler?" (Who is speaking?) When it asks who is spoken to, say: "Hvem taler du med?" (To whom are you speaking?) To ask about a thing, use "hvad" (what) instead: "Hvad spiser du?" (What are you eating?)

sentence.da: **Hvem** er din lærer?
sentence.en: Who is your teacher?

hvem som helst.explanation: "Hvem som helst" means "anyone". To say anything, use "hvad som helst" (anything) instead: "Jeg spiser hvad som helst" (I eat anything).

forms.da: Hvem som helst kan være med.

sentence.da: I dag kan **hvem som helst** lære at svømme.
sentence.en: Today anyone can learn to swim.

hver.explanation: "Hver" means "every". Put it before a word that takes "en", such as "en dag" (a day): "hver dag" (every day). For a word that takes "et", use "hvert" instead: "hvert år" (every year).

sentence.da: Jeg løber **hver** morgen.
sentence.en: I run every morning.

hver dag.explanation: "Hver dag" means "every day". It is built from "hver" (every) and "dag" (day). To say every second day, put "anden" (other) between them: "hver anden dag" (every other day).

sentence.da: Jeg drikker kaffe **hver dag**.
sentence.en: I drink coffee every day.

hverken.explanation: "Hverken" means "neither". It is used with "eller" (nor) as a pair: "hverken A eller B" (neither A nor B). To say you have neither of two things, say: "Jeg har hverken tid eller penge" (I have neither time nor money).

forms.da: hverken i dag eller i morgen

sentence.da: Jeg vil **hverken** have kaffe eller te.
sentence.en: I want neither coffee nor tea.

hverken…eller.explanation: "Hverken…eller" means "neither…nor". To say you have neither of two things, put "hverken" before the first and "eller" before the second: "Jeg har hverken tid eller penge" (I have neither time nor money). Do not add "ikke" (not), because the sentence already says no.

forms.da: hverken i dag eller i morgen

sentence.da: Kaffe eller te? **Hverken…eller**, tak. Jeg tager vand.
sentence.en: Coffee or tea? Neither, thanks. I will have water.

hvert.explanation: "Hvert" means "every". Put it before a word that takes "et", such as "et år" (a year): "hvert år" (every year). For a word that takes "en", use "hver" instead: "hver dag" (every day).

sentence.da: Vi rejser **hvert** år til Sverige.
sentence.en: We travel to Sweden every year.

hvid.explanation: "Hvid" means "white". It also starts "hvidløg" (garlic), which is literally white onion.

sentence.da: Sneen er kold og **hvid**.
sentence.en: The snow is cold and white.

hvidløg.explanation: "Hvidløg" means "garlic". It is built from "hvid" (white) and "løg" (onion). To count garlic, use "et fed" (a clove): "to fed hvidløg" (two cloves of garlic).

sentence.da: **Hvidløg** er hvidt og lugter stærkt.
sentence.en: Garlic is white and smells strong.

hvilke.explanation: "Hvilke" means "which". Put it before a word that names more than one thing: "hvilke skoler" (which schools). To ask about one thing that takes "en", use "hvilken": "hvilken bil" (which car). For one thing that takes "et", use "hvilket": "hvilket hus" (which house).

sentence.da: **Hvilke** sko vil du have?
sentence.en: Which shoes do you want?

hvilken.explanation: "Hvilken" means "which". Put it before a word that takes "en", such as "en bil" (a car): "Hvilken bil vil du have?" (Which car do you want?) For a word that takes "et", use "hvilket" instead: "Hvilket hus?" (Which house?) When no word follows, use "hvad" (what): "Hvad vil du have?" (What do you want?)

sentence.da: **Hvilken** farve kan du bedst lide?
sentence.en: Which color do you like best?

hvilket.explanation: "Hvilket" means "which". Put it before a word that takes "et", such as "et land" (a country): "Hvilket land kommer du fra?" (Which country are you from?) For a word that takes "en", use "hvilken" instead: "Hvilken bil?" (Which car?)

sentence.da: **Hvilket** hus er dit?
sentence.en: Which house is yours?

hvis.explanation: "Hvis" means "if". To say a condition, put "hvis" before it: "Hvis jeg har tid, kommer jeg" (If I have time, I will come). Do not mix it up with "om" (whether): "Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer" (I do not know whether he is coming).

sentence.da: Jeg bliver hjemme, **hvis** det regner.
sentence.en: I stay home if it rains.

hvis jeg var dig.explanation: "Hvis jeg var dig" means "if I were you". To give advice, start with it and then say what you would do: "Hvis jeg var dig, ville jeg ringe til ham" (If I were you, I would call him). The verb "var" (was) is used here where English says "were".

forms.da: Hvis jeg var dig, ville jeg vente.
forms.en: If I were you, I would wait.

sentence.da: **Hvis jeg var dig**, ville jeg blive hjemme.
sentence.en: If I were you, I would stay home.

hvor.explanation: "Hvor" means "where". To ask "how" about a quality or an amount, put "hvor" before the word: "hvor gammel" (how old), "hvor mange" (how many).

sentence.da: **Hvor** er stationen?
sentence.en: Where is the station?

hvor er toilettet?.explanation: "Hvor er toilettet?" means "Where is the restroom?". It is built from "hvor" (where), "er" (is) and "toilettet" (the toilet), where the ending "-et" means "the".

sentence.da: Undskyld, **hvor er toilettet?**
sentence.en: Excuse me, where is the restroom?

hvor gammel er du?.explanation: "Hvor gammel er du?" means "How old are you?". It is built from "hvor" (how), "gammel" (old), "er" (are) and "du" (you). To say your age, you can leave out "gammel": "Jeg er tyve år" (I am twenty years old).

sentence.da: Anna, **hvor gammel er du?**
sentence.en: Anna, how old are you?

hvor kommer du fra?.explanation: "Hvor kommer du fra?" means "Where are you from?". Literally, it asks where you come from. To answer, say: "Jeg kommer fra England" (I come from England). The word "fra" (from) stays at the end of the question, as in English.

forms.en: Where do you all come from?

sentence.da: Hej, **hvor kommer du fra?**
sentence.en: Hi, where are you from?

hvor meget koster det?.explanation: "Hvor meget koster det?" means "How much does it cost?". Word by word, it is "how much costs it". To ask about weight, use the same start with another verb: "Hvor meget vejer det?" (How much does it weigh?)

forms.en: How much does it cost? (for an en-word thing)

sentence.da: Jeg vil købe brødet. **Hvor meget koster det?**
sentence.en: I want to buy the bread. How much does it cost?

hvor som helst.explanation: "Hvor som helst" means "anywhere". The ending "som helst" also follows other question words: "hvem som helst" (anyone), "hvad som helst" (anything) and "hvornår som helst" (any time).

forms.da: Du kan bo hvor som helst.

sentence.da: Du kan sidde **hvor som helst** i rummet.
sentence.en: You can sit anywhere in the room.

hvordan.explanation: "Hvordan" means "how". To ask how old someone is, use "hvor" (how) before the word instead: "Hvor gammel er du?" (How old are you?) To ask how many, do the same: "Hvor mange børn har du?" (How many children do you have?)

sentence.da: **Hvordan** kommer jeg til stationen?
sentence.en: How do I get to the station?

hvordan går det?.explanation: "Hvordan går det?" means "How's it going?". Literally, it is "how goes it". To ask the other person back after you answer, add "og dig?" (and you?): "Det går godt, og dig?" (It's going well, and you?)

sentence.da: Hej Anna, **hvordan går det?**
sentence.en: Hi Anna, how's it going?

hvordan har du det?.explanation: "Hvordan har du det?" means "How are you?". Literally, it is "how have you it". To answer, say "Jeg har det godt" (I'm doing well) or "Fint, tak" (Fine, thanks).

sentence.da: Hej Peter! **Hvordan har du det?**
sentence.en: Hi Peter! How are you?

hvorefter.explanation: "Hvorefter" means "after which". It is built from "hvor" (which) and "efter" (after). To join two events in a simpler way, use "og så" (and then): "Hun lukkede bogen, og så slukkede hun lyset" (She closed the book, and then she turned off the light).

forms.en: after which it began to rain

sentence.da: Hun lukkede bogen, **hvorefter** hun slukkede lyset og sov.
sentence.en: She closed the book, after which she turned off the light and slept.

hvorfor.explanation: "Hvorfor" means "why". To give a reason, start your answer with "fordi" (because): "Hvorfor kommer du ikke?" "Fordi jeg er syg." (Why aren't you coming? Because I am sick.)

sentence.da: **Hvorfor** er du så glad?
sentence.en: Why are you so happy?

hvorfra.explanation: "Hvorfra" means "from where". It is built from "hvor" (where) and "fra" (from). The word "fra" (from) also ends the question "Hvor kommer du fra?" (Where do you come from?)

forms.en: Where does the bus come from?

sentence.da: **Hvorfra** kommer din ven?
sentence.en: Where does your friend come from?

hvorimod.explanation: "Hvorimod" means "whereas". To contrast two statements, put it after a comma before the second one: "Jeg drikker kaffe, hvorimod hun drikker te" (I drink coffee, whereas she drinks tea). To say two things happen at the same time, use "mens" (while) instead: "Jeg læser, mens du sover" (I read while you sleep).

sentence.da: Jeg bor i byen, **hvorimod** min søster bor på landet.
sentence.en: I live in the city, whereas my sister lives in the country.

hvornår.explanation: "Hvornår" means "when" in a question. To say "when" in the middle of a sentence about the future, use "når" (when): "Jeg ringer, når jeg kommer hjem" (I will call when I get home). To say "when" about one finished event in the past, use "da" (when): "Jeg var glad, da du kom" (I was happy when you came).

sentence.da: **Hvornår** åbner butikken?
sentence.en: When does the store open?

hvorved.explanation: "Hvorved" means "whereby". It is built from "hvor" (where) and "ved" (by). To introduce the result of an action, put it after a comma that follows the action: "Han trykkede på knappen, hvorved døren gik op" (He pressed the button, whereby the door opened).

sentence.da: Hun skrev under, **hvorved** aftalen blev gyldig.
sentence.en: She signed, whereby the agreement became valid.

hvorvidt.explanation: "Hvorvidt" means "whether". It sounds formal. In everyday speech, use "om" (whether): "Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer" (I do not know whether he is coming).

forms.da: Jeg ved ikke, hvorvidt han kommer
forms.en: I do not know whether he is coming

forms.da: spørgsmålet er hvorvidt det er muligt
forms.en: the question is whether it is possible

sentence.da: Politiet undersøger, **hvorvidt** manden har sagt sandheden.
sentence.en: The police are investigating whether the man has told the truth.

hygge.explanation: "Hygge" means "cozy". It is a Danish idea of a warm, relaxed time with other people, candles and food. To say you are having a cozy time, use "at hygge sig" (to have a cozy time): "Vi hygger os" (We are having a cozy time).

forms.en: We have a cozy time at home

sentence.da: Vi tænder lys og har **hygge** hjemme.
sentence.en: We light candles and have a cozy time at home.

hyggelig.explanation: "Hyggelig" means "cozy". It comes from "hygge" (a cozy time). To say a person is nice to be around, use it too: "Han er hyggelig" (He is nice to be around).

sentence.da: Det var en **hyggelig** aften.
sentence.en: It was a cozy evening.

hyggeligt at møde dig.explanation: "Hyggeligt at møde dig" means "nice to meet you". Literally, it is "cozy to meet you". To reply, say "i lige måde" (likewise).

sentence.da: Jeg hedder Maja. **Hyggeligt at møde dig.**
sentence.en: I'm Maja. Nice to meet you.

hyppig.explanation: "Hyppig" means "frequent". To describe how someone does something, use "hyppigt" (frequently): "Han besøger os hyppigt" (He visits us frequently).

sentence.da: Forkølelse er en **hyppig** sygdom om vinteren.
sentence.en: A cold is a frequent illness in the winter.

hysterisk.explanation: "Hysterisk" means "hysterical". To say something is extremely funny, put it before "sjov" (funny): "hysterisk sjov" (hilariously funny).

sentence.da: Hun blev **hysterisk** af skræk og begyndte at skrige.
sentence.en: She became hysterical from fright and began to scream.

hytteost.explanation: "Hytteost" means "cottage cheese". It is built from "hytte" (cottage) and "ost" (cheese). The word "ost" also ends "smøreost" (cheese you spread on bread).

sentence.da: **Hytteost** er en hvid ost med små klumper.
sentence.en: Cottage cheese is a white cheese with small lumps.

håb.explanation: "Håb" means "a hope". To say you hope for something, use the verb "at håbe" (to hope): "Jeg håber, det virker" (I hope it works).

sentence.da: Der er stadig **håb** for holdet.
sentence.en: There is still hope for the team.

håbefuld.explanation: "Håbefuld" means "hopeful". It is built from "håb" (hope) and the ending "-fuld" (full of). The same ending is in "smertefuld" (painful).

sentence.da: Hun er **håbefuld** og tror på en lykkelig slutning.
sentence.en: She is hopeful and believes in a happy ending.

håbløs.explanation: "Håbløs" means "hopeless". The ending "-løs" means "without", as in "hjemløs" (homeless). To say you are very bad at something, use it too: "Jeg er håbløs til matematik" (I am hopeless at math).

sentence.da: Situationen virker **håbløs**, og alle har givet op.
sentence.en: The situation seems hopeless, and everyone has given up.

håndbagage.explanation: "Håndbagage" means "carry-on luggage". It is built from "hånd" (hand) and "bagage" (luggage). For the bags you hand in at check-in, say "indchecket bagage" (checked luggage): "Jeg har to stykker indchecket bagage" (I have two pieces of checked luggage).

sentence.da: Jeg har kun **håndbagage** i flyet.
sentence.en: I only have carry-on luggage on the plane.

håndbold.explanation: "Håndbold" means "handball". It is built from "hånd" (hand) and "bold" (ball). To talk about the sport, leave out the article: "Jeg spiller håndbold" (I play handball). To talk about the ball, use "en håndbold" (a handball): "Jeg kaster en håndbold" (I throw a handball).

sentence.da: **Håndbold** spilles med hænderne og en bold.
sentence.en: Handball is played with the hands and a ball.

hår.explanation: "Hår" means "a hair". Without an article, it means the hair on a head: "Jeg vasker mit hår" (I wash my hair). It starts other words, such as "hårfarve" (hair color).

sentence.da: Hun har langt **hår**.
sentence.en: She has long hair.

hård.explanation: "Hård" means "hard", as in firm and not soft. To say a job is tough, use it too: "et hårdt job" (a tough job). For "hard" meaning "difficult", use "svær" (difficult) instead: "en svær opgave" (a difficult task).

sentence.da: Stenen er **hård** og kold.
sentence.en: The stone is hard and cold.

hårdhudet.explanation: "Hårdhudet" means "thick-skinned". It is built from "hård" (hard) and "hud" (skin), with the ending "-et".

sentence.da: Kritik går ikke ind på ham, fordi han er **hårdhudet**.
sentence.en: Criticism does not get to him because he is thick-skinned.

hævet.explanation: "Hævet" means "swollen". It comes from the verb "at hæve" (to raise). To say dough has risen, use the same word: "hævet dej" (risen dough).

sentence.da: Jeg faldt på trappen, og nu er min fod **hævet**.
sentence.en: I fell on the stairs, and now my foot is swollen.

hævn.explanation: "Hævn" means "revenge". To say someone takes revenge, use "at tage hævn" (to take revenge): "Han tog hævn" (He took revenge). The verb is "at hævne" (to avenge): "Hun vil hævne sin bror" (She wants to avenge her brother).

sentence.da: Han søgte **hævn**, fordi de havde ødelagt hans firma.
sentence.en: He sought revenge because they had ruined his company.

hø.explanation: "Hø" means "hay". Do not mix it up with "halm" (straw): "Hesten sover på halm" (The horse sleeps on straw).

sentence.da: Om vinteren får køerne **hø**, fordi der ikke er frisk græs.
sentence.en: In winter, the cows get hay because there is no fresh grass.

høfeber.explanation: "Høfeber" means "hay fever". It is built from "hø" (hay) and "feber" (fever). The word "feber" also stands alone: "Jeg har feber" (I have a fever).

sentence.da: Om foråret har jeg **høfeber** og klør i øjnene.
sentence.en: In spring, I have hay fever and itchy eyes.

høflig.explanation: "Høflig" means "polite". To say how someone speaks, use "høfligt" (politely): "Hun taler høfligt" (She speaks politely).

sentence.da: Han er altid **høflig** og siger tak.
sentence.en: He is always polite and says thanks.

høflighed.explanation: "Høflighed" means "politeness". It is built from "høflig" (polite) and the ending "-hed", which turns a describing word into a noun: "fri" (free) becomes "frihed" (freedom).

sentence.da: Han sagde tak af **høflighed**.
sentence.en: He said thanks out of politeness.

høj.explanation: "Høj" means "tall". To say how loud someone speaks, use "højt" (loudly): "Tal højt" (Speak loudly).

sentence.da: Giraffen er meget **høj**.
sentence.en: The giraffe is very tall.

højlydt.explanation: "Højlydt" means "loud". It is built from "høj" (high) and "lyd" (sound). To say how someone does something, use it after the verb: "Hun lo højlydt" (She laughed loudly).

sentence.da: Der var en **højlydt** diskussion i klassen.
sentence.en: There was a loud discussion in the class.

højre.explanation: "Højre" means "right", the opposite of left. To say turn right, use "til højre" (to the right): "Drej til højre" (Turn right).

sentence.da: Jeg skriver med min **højre** hånd.
sentence.en: I write with my right hand.

højst.explanation: "Højst" means "at most". To say "highly" before a describing word, use it too: "højst interessant" (highly interesting).

sentence.da: Hun er **højst** tyve år gammel.
sentence.en: She is at most twenty years old.

højtidelig.explanation: "Højtidelig" means "solemn". To say how someone speaks, use "højtideligt" (solemnly): "Hun talte højtideligt" (She spoke solemnly).

sentence.da: Ceremonien var **højtidelig**, og alle var klædt fint på.
sentence.en: The ceremony was solemn and everyone was dressed up.

hørelse.explanation: "Hørelse" means "hearing", as in the ability to hear. To say you listen to something on purpose, use "at lytte" (to listen): "Jeg lytter til musik" (I listen to music).

sentence.da: Efter mange år på fabrikken er hans **hørelse** blevet dårlig.
sentence.en: After many years at the factory, his hearing has become bad.

høretelefoner.explanation: "Høretelefoner" means "headphones". It is built from "at høre" (to hear) and "telefon" (phone). To say one set, use "et par" (a pair): "Jeg har købt et par høretelefoner" (I have bought a pair of headphones).

sentence.da: Jeg lytter til musik i mine **høretelefoner**.
sentence.en: I listen to music in my headphones.
